new.title: An Adaptive Reduced Speed of Light Approximation
new.summary: The reduced speed of light approximation (RSLA) is a common approach in radiation-hydrodynamic (RHD) simulations of non-relativistic systems where the gas speed $v_{\rm gas} \ll c$. In the RSLA one eases the severe time step constraint imposed by the speed of light $c$ by replacing it with a reduced value $\hat{c}$ chosen so that $v_{\rm gas} \ll \hat{c} \ll c$. This approach works well in flows with low or moderate optical depth, but fails in optically thick media, where it makes thermal relaxation too slow and gives incorrect RHD wave modes. Here we propose an Adaptive Reduced Speed of Light Approximation (ARSA) that removes these problems by replacing the global speed reduction factor $\phi_0 \equiv \hat{c}/c$ with a local, cell-by-cell reduction factor $\phi$ derived from a von Neumann stability analysis of the implicit-explicit update used by modern two-moment RHD codes. The resulting limiter has no tunable parameters, can be computed using only local operations, and improves on the classic RSLA by allowing $\phi \to 1$ in cells where a reduced speed of light is not required because the exchange with the gas damps unstable modes, allowing recovery of the correct thermal relaxation and wave-damping rates in highly-opaque regions. We compare ARSA to the classic RSLA in a range of standard RHD test problems, and show that in opaque regions where gas holds most of the heat capacity the ARSA is much more accurate than the RSLA at the same time step, or that it can achieve the same accuracy as the RSLA with up to 100 times fewer time steps. However, gains are limited in regions where radiation holds a large share of the heat capacity, as it does in some astrophysical systems.

new.title: Astrophysical Constraints for Bosonic Dark Matter in and Around Quark Stars
new.summary: We investigate the structure, stability, and mass-radius relations of compact stars composed of quark matter within the non-ideal MIT Bag Model mixed with self-interacting bosonic dark matter with a $\phi^n$ self-interaction potential. By solving the coupled two-fluid Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations for boson masses between 200 MeV and 1 GeV and self-interaction strengths with $n=4$ and $n=40$, we show that strong self-interactions and higher boson masses enhance the stability of compact star configurations at high central pressures, though they reduce maximum overall masses. Ultra-compact solutions with $C \ge 1/3$ capable of mimicking black holes are significantly restricted compared to hadronic models, emerging only for strong self-interactions and dark matter fractions exceeding 90\%. Depending on the parameters, the compact stars form either extended dark matter halos or compact cores: stronger self-interactions and higher boson masses suppress the radial extension to favor compact cores of dark matter. Matching our models against observational constraints highlights PSR J1614$-$2230 and XTE J1814$-$338 as potential window of opportunity for dark matter detection. Notably, XTE J1814$-$338 could confirm a dark sector, given its requirement for light boson masses ($m_b \approx 200\text{--}300\text{ MeV}$) and strongly DM-dominated configurations.

new.title: EP241206a: A Sub-kilosecond X-Ray Flare Possibly from an Active Galactic Nucleus with a Flux Increase over 3 Orders of Magnitude
new.summary: EP241206a is a fast X-ray transient detected with the Wide-field X-ray Telescope (WXT) on board the Einstein Probe. The event exhibited a single-peaked soft X-ray flare with a duration of $\sim 500$ s and a peak flux of $1.0 \times 10^{-9}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ in 0.5--4 keV, spatially coincident with a spectroscopically confirmed active galactic nucleus (AGN) at $z = 0.62$. Follow-up and archival observations revealed persistent X-ray emission at a level of $\sim 5 \times 10^{-13}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$, corresponding to $L_{2-10 \mathrm{keV}} \simeq 2.3 \times 10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$ if associated with the AGN; the WXT flare reached an estimated peak isotropic-equivalent rest-frame 2--10 keV luminosity of $\sim 1.4 \times 10^{48}$ erg s$^{-1}$, implying a peak-to-persistent luminosity contrast of over 3 orders of magnitude. Optical spectroscopy detected broad Mg II and H$\beta$ emission lines, suggesting a black hole mass of $\sim 3.8 \times 10^{7} M_{\odot}$ and Eddington ratios of 0.8 at the persistent state versus an apparent peak ratio of $\sim 4.6 \times 10^{3}$ during the flare. The extremely short duration and high apparent peak luminosity favor a jet origin, likely due to magnetic reconnection in the inner regions of a relativistic jet. Alternative scenarios include a jet-in-the-jet or a gamma-ray burst occurring within the AGN disk. However, the physical association between the transient and the AGN is not firmly established; for the radio-loud and X-ray-detected AGN counterpart class, the trial-corrected chance probability is $4.9 \times 10^{-3}$. EP241206a may represent an example of a broader population of unidentified fast X-ray transients detected with WXT.

new.title: OGHReS: Discovery of a giant hub-filament system at the edge of the Galactic molecular disc
new.summary: We present the discovery and characterisation of G195.65$-$0.10 (also known as the $\lambda$-complex), a giant hub-filament system identified by the Outer Galaxy High Resolution Survey (OGHReS). The complex contains 61 spatially and kinematically coherent HiGAL clumps with a mean velocity of $V_{\rm LSR}=32.85$ km/s and a velocity dispersion between clumps of 1.97 km/s. A $Gaia$ parallax measurement of the central emission-line star MWC 137 associated with an embedded cluster gives a heliocentric distance of 5.2$^{+0.8}_{-0.6}$ kpc, placing the complex at a Galactocentric radius of 13.2 kpc. The molecular structure spans approximately $35\times63$ pc and contains $\sim 1.6\times10^{5}$ M$_\odot$ of molecular gas, including $\sim 5 \times 10^{4}$ M$_\odot$ in dense clumps. The molecular emission is organised into three prominent velocity-coherent filaments that converge on a dense central hub. Of the associated clumps, 16 are protostellar and 45 are gravitationally bound but currently starless. The protostellar clumps are significantly more concentrated towards the hub than the starless population, with median projected offsets of 6.65 and 15.83 pc, respectively. Moreover, the luminosity-to-mass ratio of the protostellar clumps decreases significantly with increasing distance from the hub, indicating that the most evolutionarily advanced sources are preferentially located in the central region. These results reveal a systematic concentration of dense gas and increasingly evolved star formation towards the hub, with organised large-scale gas motions throughout the filamentary network. The $\lambda$-complex therefore provides an unprecedented laboratory to understand hierarchical and high-mass star formation in the outer Galactic disc.

new.title: Conditions for mass-loading: Investigating jet-disk material exchange in strongly magnetised accretion flows
new.summary: Relativistic jets are produced by accreting black holes across a wide range of masses, from stellar-mass X-ray binaries to supermassive active galactic nuclei (AGN). In low-luminosity AGN, these jets are believed to be powered by strongly magnetised accretion flows, a picture supported by Event Horizon Telescope and VLBI observations of M87. The jets often exhibit high-energy flaring emission which, if partly hadronic, implies that baryons must be loaded into the jet and accelerated despite strong magnetic barriers. However, the mechanism behind this remains unclear. We present high-resolution, three-dimensional General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations of a high-spin Magnetically Arrested Disk (MAD), a strongly magnetised accretion regime. Using passive Eulerian tracers, we track the exchange of material between the jet and disk to quantify mixing. We find that magnetic flux eruptions, a hallmark of MAD accretion, expel magnetic flux tubes initially filled with jet material (expected to be pair-dominated in real systems). Through magnetic reconnection during these eruptions, this material is mixed into the disk. Crucially, the same flux tubes reconnect the disk back to the jet, allowing disk material, expected to be primarily hadronic, to infiltrate the jet sheath and boundary. This disk-to-jet injection offers a natural mass-loading mechanism that does not require the jet to be globally baryon-dominated. The resulting ejection-injection cycle may instead drive episodic hadronic acceleration, providing a viable pathway for high-energy emission in relativistic jets.

new.title: Kinetic Monte Carlo modeling of ammonium formate NH$_4^+$HCOO$^-$ and ammonium cyanate NH$_4^+$OCN$^-$ in interstellar ices
new.summary: JWST observations have revealed evidence for NH$_4^+$ in the ices of the Chamaeleon I dark molecular cloud, with HCOO$^-$ and OCN$^-$ likely counter ions. Laboratory experiments have demonstrated that ammonium formate and ammonium cyanate can form through acid-base reactions involving NH$_3$ at cryogenic temperatures. The formation of these two ammonium salts are simulated to investigate their formation in dark-cloud ices and assess their sensitivity to uncertainties in the chemical reaction network, including the recently considered HOCO-mediated pathway for CO$_2$ formation, as well as variations in the cosmic-ray ionization rate, cloud collapse timescale and density, and elemental depletion. Our modeling framework consists of microscopic kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) simulations of grain-surface chemistry augmented by UCLCHEM gas-phase and physical cloud evolution simulations. The microscopic KMC method provides for explicit simulation of the location, movement and reaction of ice species, making it particularly well-suited to model acid-base chemistry of NH$_4^+$-salt formation, occurring within the ice mantle over extended timescales. The simulations produce the canonical ice-evolution sequence, with an initially H$_2$O-rich ice followed by a layer dominated by CO and CO$_2$. Salt production is dominated by NH$_4^+$HCOO$^-$, which is found to form predominantly during the H$_2$O-rich stage as its production is limited by the availability of NH$_3$. NH$_4^+$OCN$^-$ is found to form later at the interface between the H$_2$O- and CO-rich ice when the formation of its precursor acid HNCO is enabled. Despite the variations explored, the total NH$_4^+$ abundance, particularly relative to H$_2$O, remains remarkably robust and consistent with the observed abundance. Depending on the variation, a redistribution between counterions HCOO$^-$ and OCN$^-$ is observed.

new.title: A First Look at Astrometric Outer Companions to Super-Earths and Sub-Neptunes using Gaia DR2 and DR3
new.summary: Massive outer companions (OCs) are believed to promote, inhibit, or otherwise regulate the formation and composition of inner small planets (ISPs) both in the solar system and in exoplanetary systems. To assess how, we leverage calibrated absolute astrometry from Gaia DR2-DR3 of 7,321 FGKM dwarfs and present measurements of the relative occurrence rate of OCs in systems hosting known ISPs (i.e. P(OC$|$ISP)/P(OC)), including systems with inner super-Earths only, inner sub-Neptunes only, and across a range of spectral types and stellar metallicities. We search for OCs in pairs of planet and reference stellar samples using the orbital fitting framework Octofitter and characterize the occurrence of OCs in mass--semi-major axis space under a Bayesian hierarchical model. We find an excess of OCs in systems with ISPs ($1.77\pm0.49$), independently supporting results from radial velocity surveys for the first time using astrometry. We recover similar excesses in both super-Earth (SE; $2.02\pm0.52$) and sub-Neptune systems (SN; $1.97\pm0.50$), highlighting that OCs do not inhibit the formation of ISPs, regardless of planet type. We argue that the consistency across SE and SN systems supports ex-situ formation, wherein ISPs form rapidly at larger separations prior to OCs opening disk gaps, thus providing evidence of Type I migration of SEs and SNs. We also evaluate how these results vary across stellar mass and metallicity, finding that M dwarfs exhibit an OC excess that is $1.41\pm0.78\times$ stronger than that around FGK dwarfs, and not finding a significant dependence on metallicity, contrary to previous radial velocity surveys.

new.title: The JWST Sub-Jupiters Survey: Observed Sensitivities to the Wide-Separation, Cold, Sub-Jupiter Exoplanet Population
new.summary: We present a sensitivity analysis of three recent JWST direct imaging programs (GO-4050, GO-5835, and SURVEY-6005) designed to build a demographic study of sub-Jupiter mass ($0.1 - 1$ M$_{\mathrm{J}}$) exoplanets in nearby young associations and moving groups. We find that these programs are sensitive to sub-Saturn to Jupiter mass exoplanets with effective temperature (T$_\mathrm{eff}$) as low as $\lesssim 250$ K, already at $\sim 2$ arcsec. A comparison with the SHINE survey confirms that the improvements in mass sensitivity provided by JWST high-contrast imaging surveys outpace current ground observation for masses $\lesssim 1$ M$_{\mathrm{J}}$ and separations between $\sim20-500$ au, opening up a novel parameter space to explore. Overall, this analysis provides a robust framework for interpreting future exoplanet detections. By correlating photometrically derived properties (e.g. mass, $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and separation) with theoretical model predictions, we show how the access to potentially low detectable masses (sub-Saturn to Jupiter) strongly depends on the expected atmospheric chemistry of the exoplanet population.

new.title: Gaia as a 0.1 arcsec point-source survey across the sky: dynamical scene reconstruction from one-dimensional scans
new.summary: Gaia has observed every detected source on the sky 50 to 100 times, each time through a window of about 1 by 2 arcseconds at a different scan angle. The resulting one-dimensional flux profiles to be released in Gaia DR4 encode the two-dimensional arrangement of nearby point sources at ~0.1 arcsecond resolution. Repeated observations also constrain their relative motion. We present a method to model the scene with a mixture of moving point sources. Complementing Gaia DPAC's source-environment reconstruction, our approach focuses on close, blended companions and models their relative motion. We first fit each window with a few point sources and obtain their along-scan positions. We then triangulate these positions from different scan angles to identify candidate sources on the sky. A joint forward model of all windows measures positions, fluxes, relative proper motions, and parallax differences, even for blended components. In simulations, we recover companions at separations smaller than the instrumental profile width. For a moving companion at ~75 mas separation with a flux ratio of ~0.2, we obtain a separation precision of ~0.1 mas and a relative proper-motion precision of ~0.1 mas/yr per component, even in a scene contaminated by a third source. These precisions assume a known instrumental profile and independent Gaussian noise. We also recover differential parallax for a chance-aligned source. Modeling nearby contaminants prevents significant biases. With a Gaia-like instrumental profile, sampling and scan law, we show a sensitivity of ~5 mag in contrast at separations of 50-150 mas, and we discuss its dependence on the color term of Gaia's line-spread function. The method could extend the census of close companions and provide relative astrometry, and so dynamical information, along short orbital arcs. External measurements could also guide retrospective searches in Gaia's windows.

new.title: X-ray Flare Evolution and Changing-Look Nature of the TeV Blazar OQ 334
new.summary: The blazar OQ 334 (B2 1420+326, z = 0.682) is one of the few jetted AGN with repeated changing-look (CL) transitions between FSRQ and BL Lac states. We present a multi-wavelength study covering 2017 December to 2024 September, focusing on three X-ray flares observed with Swift-XRT (X1: 2019 June 26--July 24, X2: 2020 January 4--February 21, X3: 2024 June 24--August 2) and on the spectral properties of the CL states. The spectrum hardens from flare to flare, with $\Gamma$ decreasing from $1.97 \pm 0.09$ to $1.71 \pm 0.04$ and $1.34 \pm 0.06$, while the hysteresis evolves from an initial clockwise loop, consistent with cooling-dominated emission, to multi-loop trajectories in the later flares. The X-ray spectra separate the CL states, with FSRQ states hardest ($\Gamma_X \approx 1.3$--$1.5$), BL Lac states softest ($\Gamma_X \approx 1.8$--$2.4$), and transition states intermediate. Within the CL states, flux and photon index are positively correlated ($r = 0.59$, $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}$), producing a softer-when-brighter trend. The first two flares coincide with FSRQ $\rightarrow$ BL Lac transitions, whereas the third, the brightest, remains FSRQ-like. One-zone leptonic modelling of the broadband SEDs reproduces the flares with a weak, nearly constant magnetic field and a particle-dominated region, and the X-ray emission evolves from a substantial synchrotron contribution in the first flare to complete inverse-Compton dominance in the third. The X-ray band traces the changing balance between the synchrotron and inverse-Compton components in the flares and provides a sensitive probe of the CL behaviour of the source.

new.title: Two new Li-rich dwarf stars in M 4: abundance patterns and possible origins
new.summary: Context. Li-rich stars are rare, and only 16 are known in globular clusters (GCs), spanning evolutionary stages from the main sequence turnoff to the red giant branch. Their origin is still debated, but GCs provide a unique environment to discriminate among proposed mechanisms for Li enrichment. Aims. We aim to characterise two newly discovered Li-rich dwarf stars, 44606 and 58195, in the GC M 4 (NGC 6121) and investigate their origin among the formation channels proposed in the literature. The previously known Li-rich star in the cluster, namely 37934, was re-analyzed for comparison. Methods. We performed a standard abundance analysis based on 1D model atmospheres in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) on high-resolution Ultraviolet and Visual Echelle Spectrograph (UVES). We measured the projected rotational velocity and searched for chromospheric activity. Results. We derive A(Li)= 2.58, 2.51 dex for stars 44606 and 58195, respectively, significantly different from the A(Li) distribution of normal dwarfs in M 4. For the known Li-rich star 37934, we obtain A(Li)= 3.01 dex, consistent with previous work. We estimate detailed abundances of 24 species (Li, C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, S, K, Ca, Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Sr, Y, Zr, Ba, and Nd) in the three stars. None of our targets show detectable rotational broadening or chromospheric activity. Conclusions. The Li-rich stars analysed here are unevolved, ruling out in-situ Li production. Planet engulfment is very unlikely in GCs, and we detect no present-day rotation or activity. By exclusion, the most plausible remaining scenarios involve different types of interaction with a companion, including dynamical interactions, mass transfer, and mergers. Currently, we have not detected a companion.

new.title: Gravitational Waves from Population III Black Hole Mergers in Primordial Gas Disks: Constraining Astrophysical Scenarios with the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna and the Einstein Telescope
new.summary: The first generation of metal-free Population III (Pop~III) stars provides a possible formation channel for the black hole (BH) seeds in the early Universe. Their remnants may grow through gas accretion and mergers, producing gravitational wave (GW) signals detectable by future observatories. We develop a semi-analytical model of fragmentation in a primordial self-gravitating gas disk within minihaloes at $z > 15$, motivated by high-resolution cosmological simulations. The resulting Pop~III stars form around a central primary, some leaving massive BH remnants that migrate towards the central BH through dynamical friction from gas and dark matter, while the central BH grows through accretion and mergers. For a $10^6~{\rm M_\odot}$ halo at $z=20$, we explore how the initial mass function (IMF) and BH accretion efficiency affect detectability with the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) and the Einstein Telescope (ET). We find that both detectors can potentially reveal mergers of Pop III remnant BHs, but favor different astrophysical conditions. LISA pinpoints more massive central BHs ($\sim10^3$-$10^4 {\rm M_\odot}$), grown rapidly through mutual mergers alongside efficient gas accretion ($f_{\rm Edd}=1$), and a relatively top-heavy IMF ($\alpha=0.8$). In contrast, detectability with ET favors lower-mass BHs, with less efficient accretion ($f_{\rm Edd}=0.01$) and a steeper IMF ($\alpha=1.5$). These results highlight the potential of LISA and ET to probe Pop~III BH formation, growth, and mergers across different regions of parameter spaces, jointly constraining Pop~III star formation and early BH seed evolution.

new.title: Compositions of Exoplanetary Debris Shaped by Milky Way Stellar Abundance Patterns
new.summary: Galactic chemical evolution (GCE) predicts large-scale variations in exoplanet compositions with host star elemental abundances, reflecting the Milky Way's history of star formation and elemental enrichment from stellar feedback. We investigate the impact of GCE on the compositions of exoplanetary bodies using polluted white dwarfs (WDs), which probe the bulk elemental abundances of planetary debris. Using a literature sample of 70 polluted WDs, we calculate iron mass fractions for the accreted bodies and compare these to tracers of the WD progenitor's initial abundances, including age and kinematics. We demonstrate predicted trends using a sample of main sequence stars, and we show that these are generally reflected in the polluted WD sample. In particular, H-dominated WDs show preferentially larger iron mass fractions amongst younger and less dynamically excited systems. This trend is weaker amongst He-dominated WDs, and we show that this may be attributed to uncertainties in their observed phases of accretion. Continuing to combine WD pollution compositions with stellar parameters and kinematics could be a valuable way to constrain large-scale versus local drivers of planetary compositions.

new.title: Rest-frame annihilation lines of $\sim70$ GeV WIMPs in 23,000 stacked galaxy clusters
new.summary: Weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) annihilation features were reported as a 43 GeV line in three Fermi-LAT galaxy clusters ($\mathtt{S}_3$), as triad $\{\gamma\gamma, \gamma Z,\gamma h\}$ lines from $\sim70$ GeV WIMPs in LAT data cross-correlated ($\mathtt{C}_{\mathtt{W}}$) with western eROSITA X-rays, and as a nonad (combining three triads) of two cross-annihilating WIMPs in $\mathtt{C}_{\mathtt{W}}$. A blind scan of LAT 16.3-year data around 23,343 high-latitude clusters in their rest frames finds three triads, at 70 GeV ($2.8\sigma$ trial-corrected, henceforth), $72$ GeV ($1.3\sigma$; strengthening to $2.7\sigma$ if mass-fixed by $\mathtt{S}_3$, $4.0\sigma$ combined with $\mathtt{C}_{\mathtt{W}}$ masked around the clusters, $5.7\sigma$ if also combined with $\mathtt{S}_3$), and 74-75 GeV: a triplet not only rare ($3.5\sigma$) but also forming a $\{70,74\}$ GeV nonad ($3.4\sigma$; strengthening to $4.0\sigma$, $4.6\sigma$, and $6.1\sigma$, respectively). The spectral features, robust in and out of the $\mathtt{C}_{\mathtt{W}}$ region and $\mathtt{S}_3$ clusters, appear in all Galactic quadrants and only in the cluster rest frame (vanishing upon redshift rescaling or permutation), fade away from cluster centers, are absent from their surrounding stacked fields, and like $\mathtt{C}_{\mathtt{W}}$ indicate intrinsic few $10^{-19}$ cm$^3$ s$^{-1}$ cross sections (uncorrected) across samples. All features are largely explained by cross-annihilating $69.7^{+0.4}_{-1.0}$ and $74.5^{+1.1}_{-0.6}$ GeV WIMPs.

cross.title: Composition-dependent ultralight dark matter detection with a tetrahedral superconducting gravity gradiometer
cross.summary: Tetrahedral superconducting gravity gradiometers designed as full-tensor gravitational-wave detectors, such as the ground-based mSOGRO design and the proposed lunar LANGO observatory, reconstruct the acceleration-gradient tensor from four test masses. We show that giving the four test masses two compositions in a $2+2$ arrangement adds a composition-dependent ultralight dark matter (ULDM) channel to that same tensor readout, with no separate dark-matter sensor and no dark-matter-specific readout. A coherently oscillating scalar accelerates each mass in proportion to its dilaton charge, and the tensor reconstruction leaves the charges only in a mean, rejected with the common mode, and a single vector $\qv$ proportional to the charge contrast $\Delta\abaralpha_{AB}$ between the two materials. The response is the rank-one tensor $\K_{\ULDM}(t)=\gv_\phi(t)\otimes\qv$, whose amplitude is set by the halo, independent of $m_\phi$. The axis of $\qv$ is fixed in advance by the material assignment, so the response obeys the null condition $\K_{\ULDM}(\mathbf{I}-\Pq)=0$ at every instant, for any $\gv_\phi$ including a virialized field with a stochastic gradient---an exact tensor discriminator against gravitational-wave signals; for a single composition $\qv=0$. With the gravitational-wave noise model, the coupling sensitivity for copper and lead test masses reaches $d_{\hat m}-d_g\simeq3.4\times10^{-8}$ for the baseline instrument and $4.9\times10^{-10}$ with upgraded accelerometers. The rank-one factorization and the null condition are summarized in a companion Letter; the present paper gives the derivations and the detector-level analysis.

cross.title: Microcausality Bounds on Dispersion Laws
cross.summary: Microcausality holds in any state, including those that spontaneously break Lorentz invariance, and requires the poles (and other singularities) of the retarded Green's function to satisfy $\mathrm{Im}\,\omega \le |\mathrm{Im}\,k|$ throughout the complex plane. Building on the work of Heller, Serantes, Spaliński and Withers, we study its consequences for dispersion relations that are linear at small $k$, like Goldstone bosons, assuming tree-level, non-dissipative dynamics. We show that microcausality is equivalent to requiring that $k \pm \omega(k)$ be typically real functions. This yields two-sided bounds on all higher-order coefficients of $\omega(k)$ in units of its radius of convergence $R$, the scale at which the linear Goldstone description breaks down. The optimal constraints are characterised by an infinite hierarchy of Toeplitz determinants. We derive analogous bounds on $\omega^2(k)$, whose radius of convergence $\tilde R$ marks the scale at which new states must appear. The bounds shrink to zero as the sound speed $c_s$ approaches 1: for a fixed higher-derivative correction, both $R$ and $\tilde R$ become parametrically smaller than naive dimensional analysis suggests. In particular, in the EFT of Inflation all higher-derivative quadratic operators must vanish as $c_s \to 1$. We test the bounds in several models: a $U(1)$ superfluid, light in a dielectric medium, photon propagation in a strong magnetic field, colour-flavour-locked quark matter, and a homogeneous solid. Finally, we extend the bounds to gapped modes.

cross.title: Powering the Space Elevator
cross.summary: Powering the Space Elevator is a report on the work of an International Space Elevator Consortium study group tasked with determining the technology options for delivering power to the climbers on the space elevator at any altitude above Earth. The book covers options such as laser power beaming, microwave beaming, a solar-powered climber, and delivering power through the electrical conductivity of the tether. This report starts with the reference conceptual design of a climber from the 2023 study report, "The Climber/Tether Interface of the Space Elevator," and adds features to the climber that allow it to ascend or descend the elevator tether. The strengths and limitations of current technologies are identified, along with areas for future research.

cross.title: An improved statistical treatment for radioassay-based background projection incorporating part-to-part variation
cross.summary: For low background experiments, prediction of the background from radioactivity in detector components is of critical importance. Radioassays are often conducted on small samples or individual parts, which may be subject to differences in production or handling resulting in a part-to-part variation. This part-to-part variation can have an impact on the total activity and is not presently captured by the averaging methods used to evaluate radioassays. We propose a new method for the averaging of radioassays to incorporate this part-to-part variation into predictions of the total activity of parts. We also consider how to add component activities based on assays for component groups that are simulated as a single entity.

cross.title: Nonperturbative lattice simulation of the nucleation rate in thermal first-order phase transitions
cross.summary: We present a nonperturbative lattice study of vacuum decay through bubble nucleation in a three-dimensional real scalar field theory at finite temperature. The vacuum decay rate is computed by combining an expanded-ensemble multicanonical hybrid Monte Carlo approach, which samples the critical bubble configurations, with real-time Langevin dynamics, which follows the subsequent bubble evolution. We extrapolate the nucleation rate to the continuum limit and compare it with the corresponding one-loop perturbative prediction, finding a discrepancy of about \(8\%\).

cross.title: Black Hole Superradiance and the Gravitational Auger Effect
cross.summary: Black hole superradiance is a powerful probe of nature's light degrees of freedom. In the vicinity of a spinning black hole, it exponentially amplifies ultralight bosons from vacuum fluctuations to a macroscopic cloud of enormous occupation number. Observational superradiance effects - modified black-hole spins, gravitational-wave and coherent boson emission - are known to depend sensitively on bosonic self-interactions as induced by a quartic, $\lambda \phi^4$. Here we point out that purely gravitational interactions within the cloud significantly modify superradiance dynamics, through an analog of the Auger effect. Moreover, we identify nontrivial evolution of the superradiant levels beyond the first, driven by scattering into even higher levels and their radial overtones. For the QCD axion, the irreducible gravitational coupling rapidly dissipates the first superradiant level after it reaches saturation, through scalar emission and absorption by the black hole, while truncating the growth of higher levels. This can dramatically suppress the observability of continuous gravitational-wave signals or signatures in late binary inspirals. Black hole spin-down remains more robust, but for higher modes begins earlier and proceeds more slowly, requiring revision of existing limits.

cross.title: Drift of a Charged Particle in a Black Hole Magnetosphere: the Effect of Black Hole Spin
cross.summary: Sparse plasma immersed in a strong magnetic field is common in astrophysical scenarios, for which a collisionless description is more appropriate. The guiding-center approximation serves as an effective tool for describing the motion of charged particles in a strong magnetic field, revealing the drift, a sub-leading order motion that causes particles to deviate from the magnetic field lines. It is widely accepted that the charged particles drift under the induction of gravity in Newtonian framework. However, a covariant formulation of the guiding-center approximation, as well as the drift of a charged particle induced by strong gravitational field, has yet to be fully explored. As a preliminary study, we aim to analyze the drift of a single charged particle in a black hole magnetosphere via a covariant approach. Particularly, we focus on the effects of black hole spin. We first examine the drift caused by the rotation of a massive object in the Newtonian regime using the language of gravitoelectromagnetism. A covariant formula of drift is derived, which is confirmed to reduce to the Newtonian results in the weak gravitational field and low speed limit. The impact of BH spin on the drift is analyzed in detail in Kerr spacetime specifically, for which we define the drift rate whose value quantifies the significance of the drift. Our results indicate that the impact of BH spin on the drift of a charged particle in a BH magnetosphere can be comparable to that of other factors in some extreme cases.

cross.title: Bayesian Time-Varying Spectral Estimation for LISA with P-Splines
cross.summary: We model the evolutionary spectrum of a slowly time-varying process by a linear combination of products of time- and frequency-dependent B-splines, placing a Gaussian tensor-product penalty prior on the coefficients. The posterior distribution is obtained by updating the prior using a Whittle-type likelihood approximation of the Wilson-Daubechies-Meyer time-frequency coefficients. Separate regularisation in time and frequency allows non-stationary spectral structure to be inferred. An adaptive coarse-grained likelihood reduces the computational cost while preserving fine resolution around sharp spectral features. We first validate the method using repeated simulations of a locally stationary process with known spectrum, showing lower reconstruction errors and narrower posterior intervals as the sample size increases. We then apply it to a year-long simulated LISA data set with stationary instrumental single link spectra, an evolving time-delay interferometry (TDI) response, and a modulated Galactic foreground. We compare a flexible total power spectral density (PSD) model with models incorporating progressively stronger physical information and examine both continuous and gapped observations. Allowing time variation substantially improves reconstruction relative to a stationary model, while incorporating physical information about the TDI response further improves recovery, particularly near its moving spectral features. The results illustrate the trade-off between spectral flexibility, physical assumptions, and posterior uncertainty in non-stationary LISA noise estimation.

cross.title: Relativistic precession around rotating neutron stars. I. Slow rotation: Hartle--Thorne spacetimes, particle orbits and the QPOs of atoll and Z sources
cross.summary: We study the relativistic precession model (RPM) of quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in the spacetimes of slowly rotating neutron stars computed from the equation of state (EOS). For four EOSs (WFF1, G3, FSUGarnet and IOPB-I) we solve the Hartle--Thorne equations to second order in the angular velocity and compute the orbital and epicyclic frequencies of the exterior metric without expanding in the spin or the quadrupole. At $1.9\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ the spin-induced quadrupole is 2--4 times that of a black hole with the same spin; it lowers the nodal precession frequency by up to 25 per cent near the innermost stable circular orbit and limits the nodal frequency that any spin can produce. An eccentric, tilted geodesic around a $1.92\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ star spinning at 363~Hz precesses at the epicyclic rates, and the power spectrum of a hot spot on it peaks at the orbital, periastron and nodal precession frequencies. Applied to the atoll sources 4U 1636$-$53 and 4U 1728$-$34, the RPM gives masses of 2.02--$2.15\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ and 1.88--$1.92\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$. For 4U 1728$-$34 the low-frequency QPO favours stars with large moments of inertia, $I\simeq2.5\times10^{45}$~g\,cm$^{2}$. Without an EOS the QPOs give $M=1.920^{+0.014}_{-0.012}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, $j=0.162^{+0.023}_{-0.011}$ and $\bar Q=2.2^{+1.1}_{-0.8}$; a Kerr spacetime with the same nodal frequency would underestimate the moment of inertia by 22 per cent. For the Z sources GX 5$-$1 and GX 340+0 the horizontal-branch oscillations cannot be twice the nodal precession frequency for any of the four EOSs: the fits are driven to spins of 730--745~Hz and to the maximum mass.

cross.title: Scalar charge of neutron stars and accreting black holes in Starobinsky gravity: quasi-universal relations, the trace anomaly and gravitational-wave sensitivity
cross.summary: The Starobinsky scalaron is sourced by the trace of the stress--energy, so its exterior charge is set by the matter around an object and not by the object's vacuum geometry. We derive a master formula for that charge for any static, spherically symmetric source, evaluate it first for neutron stars, where the interior is known, and then for accreting black holes, where it is not. For a star the pressure subtracts: on the interior metric with the Eardley sensitivity, and the charge is a quasi-universal function of the compactness. Six realistic equations of state confirm the relation but lie above the coefficient calibrated on polytropes; the refit reproduces their mean to 0.007. The trace $\rho-3p$ changes sign in the cores of massive stars, and the charge also tracks the tidal deformability and the moment of inertia to a few parts in 1000 and 100. Solving the Einstein-frame structure equations self-consistently moves a star along this relation and leaves its charge at fixed compactness within 4 per cent of the test-field value. We compare the charge with NICER radii and the GW170817 tidal deformability, and use the published massless dipole constraint from GW230529 to calibrate a Fisher estimate of the sensitivity of a similar binary to a finite scalaron range, projected to the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer; the range is a free parameter, and the laboratory bound on pure $R+\alpha R^2$ is confronted explicitly. A vacuum black hole has q=0; a hole with a disc has $q=\sinh(m_\phi r_d)/(m_\phi r_d)$, controlled by the disc's outer edge, which makes it the counterpart in which the same integral is dominated by matter far from the centre; light is blind to the charge at leading order, and the correction beyond it is negligible for any self-consistent disc.

cross.title: Comparative Analysis of Influences of Magnetic Field Inputs on Simulating the 2017 September 10 Solar Energetic Particle Event
cross.summary: Physics-based solar energetic particle (SEP) models simulate the ambient solar wind, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and SEPs using photospheric magnetic field maps as the inner boundary condition. In this study, we select the 2017 September 10 SEP event, which produced the first ground level enhancement observed on the surfaces of both Earth and Mars, to examine how these inputs influence the modeled results. We use the SOlar wind with FIeld lines and Energetic particles (SOFIE) model suite, driven independently by the GONG and ADAPT-GONG magnetic field maps, to simulate the solar wind, CME, and SEPs from the low corona to beyond Mars' orbit. The two maps yield different open flux regions and hence different solar wind conditions, both globally comparable to in situ observations at Earth, STA, and Mars, with the GONG-driven results performing slightly better. We find that in the ADAPT-GONG-driven run, a more energetic CME flux rope propagates into a slower, wider stream, producing broader CME expansion and a more extended shock, which reaches both planets within ~4 hours of the observed arrival, while the GONG-driven run misses both arrivals. Both simulations reproduce the observed SEP fluxes at Earth within a factor of ~3, while the ADAPT-GONG-driven results compare better with observations at Mars, which connects magnetically to the shock flank. Therefore, for this event, the relative performance of the two simulations depends on the observer and observable, with SEP fluxes shaped by CME propagation through the ambient solar wind and by magnetic connectivity to the evolving shock.

cross.title: A hybrid log-likelihood-ratio statistic for single-detector SPIIR gravitational-wave searches
cross.summary: Periods with only one detector operating accounted for 13.3 percent of the third LIGO-Virgo observing run (O3) and 29.7 percent of the first part of the fourth observing run (O4a). We present the first dedicated single-detector implementation of the Summed Parallel Infinite Impulse Response (SPIIR) pipeline for binary neutron star (BNS) and neutron star-black hole (NSBH) merger searches. Our hybrid log-likelihood ratio combines signal-consistency models for non-Gaussian glitches with a profile likelihood ratio for the signal-to-noise ratio under a Gaussian-noise model. We calibrate the glitch model by source category and trigger-rate class. We assign false alarm rates (FARs) using the measured background from the same detector and analysis chunk, extrapolating its high-ranking tail. We check the FAR assignments by comparing observed and expected cumulative background counts for BNS in O3a and NSBH in O3b at LIGO Hanford (H1) and LIGO Livingston (L1). Using O3 data and the GWTC-3 injection set, we find that, at a threshold of one false alarm per two months, the BNS sensitive distances are $136.5^{+2.9}_{-3.0}$ Mpc in L1 and $120.2^{+3.1}_{-3.3}$ Mpc in H1. These central estimates are approximately 24 and 38 percent higher, respectively, than the GWTC-3 GstLAL values of $110.5^{+3.2}_{-3.4}$ Mpc and $87.2^{+3.6}_{-3.9}$ Mpc over the same data and injection parameter ranges. GstLAL provides the only published single-detector results in GWTC-3. For NSBH, SPIIR reaches $164.1^{+6.7}_{-7.3}$ Mpc in L1 and $134.9^{+6.3}_{-7.0}$ Mpc in H1, compared with $165.1^{+6.7}_{-7.3}$ Mpc and $156.0^{+5.9}_{-6.4}$ Mpc for GWTC-3 GstLAL, respectively. Targeted searches recover triggers associated with GW190425, GW200105_162426, and GW230529_181500 with assigned FARs below the same threshold.

cross.title: Probing superradiant cloud level transitions in stellar-mass black hole binaries with milli-Hertz and multiband gravitational wave observations
cross.summary: We investigate superradiant cloud level transitions in stellar-mass black hole binaries with milli-Hertz and multiband gravitational-wave observations. Under the adopted cloud formation and survival conditions, the $\lvert322\rangle\rightarrow\lvert31-1\rangle$ fine transition can imprint phase corrections in the LISA band, while Bohr transitions occurring after the milli-Hertz band observation can be probed through shifts in the merger time. Modeling the coupled cloud-orbit evolution, we find that cloud depletion can begin before resonance and that ionization can advance rather than delay coalescence. For a representative nearby binary, a vacuum injection-recovery analysis yields a cloud-mass-fraction posterior concentrated at $M_c^i/M\lesssim10^{-6}$. Comparing the LISA-predicted coalescence time with a subsequent ground-based measurement provides a complementary test of later cloud evolution. These results motivate complementary searches for ultralight bosons with milli-Hertz and multiband gravitational-wave observations.

cross.title: Triple Exchange at the Cosmological Collider in Closed Form
cross.summary: Particles with masses near the Hubble scale leave a characteristic pattern in the primordial bispectrum, turning inflation into a cosmological collider. For light fields, where this signal is largest, no closed form is known for the full shape of the quasi-single-field triple exchange. Using Feynman-integral methods, we obtain the first closed-form results, exact in the momenta, as expansions in terms of multiple polylogarithms around the massless and conformally coupled limits. We show that the template used in Planck analyses overestimates the amplitude by up to a factor of 1.8 and underestimates the mass, whereas our new template recovers both, as needed for current and upcoming CMB and galaxy surveys. We also compute the collapsed trispectrum and, combining it with the bispectrum, find that at weak mixing it bounds the self-coupling more tightly.

cross.title: Repeated Gravitational-Wave Lensing from Binary Black Holes on Eccentric and Precessing Orbits around Spinning Supermassive Black Holes
cross.summary: Gravitational waves (GWs) from a stellar-mass binary black hole (BBH) orbiting a supermassive black hole (SMBH) can experience repeated gravitational lensing as the BBH passes behind the SMBH. Our previous studies of orbit-induced GW modulation motivate this investigation of repeated lensing in evolving hierarchical triple systems. We investigate how eccentricity, inclination, and relativistic precession of the outer orbit affect successive lensing events and parameter inference. The outer orbit follows post-Newtonian dynamics, and the inspiral waveform includes moving-source effects and de Sitter precession. An event-local point-mass lensing model tracks the changing source--lens alignment and GW frequency. For a one-year LISA observation, we examine lensing-event identification, Fisher-matrix estimates of parameter uncertainties, and waveform residuals when lensing is omitted. Our results show that outer-orbit evolution changes the timing and amplification of successive lensing events and can bring initially unfavorable configurations into the lensing region. A fixed circular, nonprecessing approximation misses all lensing events for a substantial fraction of the selected lensed systems. The median fractional reductions in uncertainty are largest for the outer-orbit inclination and SMBH spin. For some systems above the adopted detection threshold, lensing-induced waveform differences persist after local adjustments to the parameters of the unlensed model. Repeated lensing can thus provide complementary constraints on SMBH properties and outer-orbit geometry in LISA observations of hierarchical BBHs.

cross.title: Simultaneous tests of post-Newtonian inspiral using GW250114 and GW250207
cross.summary: We perform the one of the most general tests of post-Newtonian (PN) inspiral in binary black holes to date by allowing all eight phase coefficients up to 3.5PN order to vary simultaneously from their general-relativistic values. Using two of the loudest binary black hole events observed to date, GW250114 and GW250207, we carry out Bayesian inference with the IMRPhenomXPHM_SpinTaylor waveform model augmented by parametrized deviations in the post-Newtonian phasing. We then identify the combinations of phase coefficients most strongly constrained by the data through a principal component analysis of the eight-dimensional deformation space. We find that the data constrain the three leading principal components beyond their priors, and that all three are consistent with the predictions of general relativity. These results demonstrate that exceptionally loud gravitational-wave events enable robust, high-dimensional tests of inspiral dynamics and provide direct access to the measurable subspace of post-Newtonian deformations.

cross.title: Directionality of low-energy electron recoils in the CYGNO experiment
cross.summary: Electron-recoil directionality can help distinguish solar-neutrino interactions from backgrounds and, together with recoil-energy measurements and three-dimensional tracking, enable neutrino-energy spectroscopy. We study the reconstruction of the initial direction of low-energy electron recoils in the CYGNO optical time-projection chamber, focusing on the 50 L LIME prototype and its high-granularity scientific CMOS (sCMOS) readout. A dedicated algorithm identifies the interaction point from the asymmetry of the track light distribution and estimates the recoil direction from the early portion of the ionization trail, before multiple scattering erases most of the directional information. The method is characterized with a detailed Monte Carlo simulation of electron recoils and detector response. Samples spanning 15 keV to 70 keV are used to optimize the algorithm parameters by minimizing the width of the reconstructed-minus-true projected-angle distribution. The projected angular response is modeled by two Gaussian components that account for its dependence on track inclination. The narrower component, associated with favorable projections approximately parallel to the Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) plane, has a width that improves from about $20^\circ$ near 20 keV to about $12^\circ$ at 60 keV. We also quantify the fraction of events in the correctly reconstructed angular core and discuss the dominant limitations of a camera-only two-dimensional measurement.

cross.title: Cosmological Collider Signals from Fermion Bubble Loops with a Chemical Potential
cross.summary: We present the first systematic analytical calculation of the local and nonlocal cosmological collider (CC) signals generated by massive fermion bubble loops in the presence of an effective chemical potential during inflation. Working in the de Sitter approximation, we investigate the four-point correlator of inflaton perturbations in the single-squeezed limit. By combining CC cutting rules, late-time expansions, and partial Mellin-Barnes (MB) techniques, we derive analytical expressions for both local and nonlocal signals. In particular, we identify two distinct contributions to the local signal, arising from spectrum and integer poles and from ultraviolet poles of the loop-momentum integral. We further investigate the three-point limit, where the separately extracted local and nonlocal contributions develop apparent folded singularities. By reorganizing the MB representation, we demonstrate that these singularities cancel in the complete signal and obtain a convergent double-MB integral suitable for numerical evaluation. Independent calculations using complementary MB representations provide nontrivial consistency checks of our results. We find that the chemical potential can significantly enhance the oscillatory signal while increasing its logarithmic oscillation frequency. Our analytical results provide a foundation for further studies of chemical-potential-enhanced fermionic CC signals, including fermion triangle loops.

cross.title: Maximum entropy reconstruction of the black hole greybody factors from its Korteweg-de Vries integrals
cross.summary: The dynamics of perturbed non-rotating black holes (BHs) can be described by master wave equations with a potential barrier. Recent work has shown that these equations possess an infinite number of symmetries generated by the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) hierarchy, leading to conserved quantities (KdV integrals) that fully determine the BH greybody factors via a moment problem. In this paper, we introduce and validate a new method to solve this moment problem using the maximum entropy principle. The method reconstructs, at each order of truncation, the least-biased transmission probability compatible with a finite set of KdV integrals, guaranteeing positivity by construction. We first validate the technique against the exactly solvable Pöschl-Teller potential. We then apply it to the Regge-Wheeler potential governing axial perturbations of a Schwarzschild BH, where no exact solution is available; the resulting reconstruction agrees closely with the fourth-order Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin (WKB) approximation across several multipoles. This is the first application of the maximum entropy method to the reconstruction of BH greybody factors, demonstrating that a modest number of KdV integrals is sufficient to recover them accurately.

cross.title: Hunting dark matter: the present and future of direct particle detection
cross.summary: The nature of dark matter remains one of the major open questions in particle physics and cosmology. Direct detection experiments aim to identify dark matter particles through their interactions with ordinary matter, but despite substantial improvements in experimental sensitivity, no conclusive detection has been achieved. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the present status and future prospects of direct particle detection, focusing on searches for dark matter particles from the Galactic halo. We introduce the theoretical framework for interpreting experimental results, including nuclear and electron scattering, collective excitations, particle absorption, and time- and direction-dependent signatures. We review the detection technologies employed in these searches, highlighting their operating principles, advantages, and limitations, as well as the calibration techniques and background mitigation strategies required to achieve high sensitivity. Particular emphasis is placed on experimental results reported since 2020, covering nuclear and electron recoil searches, annual modulation measurements, and directional detection. We also discuss experiments under construction and proposed future detectors, ranging from large-scale noble-liquid experiments to low-threshold technologies targeting sub-GeV dark matter. Finally, we examine the challenges that will shape the next generation of experiments, including the need for increasingly low energy thresholds, improved background understanding and discrimination, and the growing importance of neutrino-induced backgrounds. The diversity and complementarity of detector technologies will remain essential for exploring the dark matter parameter space and establishing the nature of any potential signal.

The top inset displays the typical simultaneous phonon and charge (left) and phonon and light (right) signals, which depend on the interacting particle, enabling background discrimination.

The sensitive volume is the Si-depleted region (shown in dark green), where the energy released by an interacting particle during the exposure period is converted into electron-hole pairs, which are efficiently collected and stored until readout. The distribution of the number of electrons accumulated per pixel is shown in the inset on the right for typical event topologies associated with different interacting particles, enabling background discrimination. A dark matter interaction would look like the cluster in the upper-left corner.

4: Illustration of a high-purity germanium detector with a point-contact geometry. The germanium crystal (shown in green) is housed in a vacuum vessel and cooled to 77 K via a cold finger. Energy deposited by an interacting particle is converted into electron-hole pairs, which are drifted and collected at the electrodes by the electric field. The inset on the right displays the typical signal shape. The time evolution of the charge signal –and its derivative, the current pulse– can be used to identify multiple site energy depositions from point-like interactions.

The energy released by a particle interaction results in the emission of scintillation photons (gray wavy arrows), typically in the visible-UV range, that propagate toward light sensors. The left and right insets display typical signal shapes from the photosensors (exemplified here by photomultiplier tubes). The signal shape depends on the scintillation time constant of the chosen target. To prevent dark events from triggering the system, two or more photosensors per module are read out in coincidence mode.

6: Illustration of a bubble chamber. The sensitive volume consists of a metastable liquid (shown in green) housed in a tight vessel, under controlled temperature and pressure. The energy released by a highly-ionizing particle interacting in the liquid can nucleate a gas bubble. This nucleation generates a sound wave (dotted lines) propagating through the liquid. The left and right insets display representative sound signal waveforms registered by piezoelectric sensors and the right-bottom inset, a bubble as viewed by the cameras under appropriate lighting.

In both concepts, scintillation light (gray wavy arrows) is detected by photosensors, such as PMTs or SiPMs. In the dual-phase detector, this prompt light constitutes the S1 signal, which is complemented by the S2 signal generated via electroluminiscence as electrons drift into the upper gas phase under an applied electric field. The top insets display typical signals for both detector concepts. In the single-phase (left), individual PMT signals allow the reconstruction of the interaction position and in the case of using argon, the scintillation pulse shape allows particle discrimination. In the dual-phase (right) the ratio between S1 and S2 signals allows for particle discrimination, while the time interval between them and the pattern of light sensor hits, the reconstruction of the interaction point.

Right: The resonator concept exploits quantum and collective excitations of 3 He superfluid medium (shown in green) excited by the interacting particles, which are measured using mechanical resonators. The scattering of quasiparticles in the resonator modifies the resonance frequency width, acting as a sensitive thermometer. cross.title: Observing Earth's ionospheric irregularities from the Moon
cross.summary: Radio signals that propagate through the Earth's ionosphere carry information about possible irregular plasma structures. Such irregularities manifest themselves as amplitude signatures that depend on the propagation and observation geometry [1, 2]. Conventional ground and low-Earth-orbit (LEO) measurements sample these effects close to Earth. Here we present a systematic characterization of terrestrial ionospheric irregularities using Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) amplitude observations from the lunar surface, at distances of approximately 356,000-398,000 km from Earth's surface [3]. Using nearly 93 h of 1-Hz lunar-surface observations of GPS L1/L5 and Galileo E1/E5a collected by the Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment (LuGRE), we reconstruct the propagation and scanning geometry to characterize the spatiotemporal signatures of amplitude and phase fluctuations. At lunar distance, the Fresnel scale approaches its finite-source limit, extending the observations to a propagation regime beyond conventional near-Earth configurations. Detrended receiver-reported carrier-to-noise density ratios (${\delta}C/N_0$) reveal pronounced polar amplitude fluctuations at both frequency bands, also visible in the original measurements. Within the regions and local times sampled, large fluctuations occur in about 30% of valid one-minute polar windows, compared with less than 5% in either the equatorial or mid-latitude band. These findings support using the lunar surface as a vantage point for studying Earth's polar ionospheric irregularities and testing how propagation and scanning relative to the magnetic field shape their amplitude signatures. Future lunar observations could extend this approach to long-term monitoring of Earth's ionospheric irregularities

cross.title: Pulsar Timing Correlations Induced by Stochastic Spin-2 Ultralight Dark Matter
cross.summary: Ultralight dark matter (ULDM) can generate time-dependent gravitational perturbations, providing a potential signal for pulsar timing arrays (PTAs). In Galactic halos, the velocity dispersion of ULDM gives rise to finite spatial coherence, which influences the correlations between pulsar timing signals. In this work, we derive the timing-residual cross-correlations induced by rapid metric oscillations of spin-2 ULDM, allowing for general polarization statistics. Under equipartition among the five polarization modes, the intrinsic angular kernel contains monopole and quadrupole components and exhibits an angular profile closely resembling that of spin-1 ULDM, suggesting a potential degeneracy between the two ULDM candidates in PTA observations.

cross.title: Detectability of Eccentric Intermediate Mass-Ratio Inspiral in the Decihertz Band
cross.summary: The proposed decihertz gravitational-wave (GW) band $(\sim 10^{-2}-1\,\Hz)$ will observe the late inspiral of intermediate mass-ratio inspirals (IMRIs), binaries with mass ratios $10^2 \lesssim q \lesssim 10^4$ that assemble dynamically in dense stellar environments and are expected to retain measurable eccentricity. Search and parameter-estimation pipelines are predominantly built around circular templates, and we test this assumption. Using black-hole perturbation theory waveforms from \textsc{FastEMRIWaveforms} for a representative IMRI ($M=10^4\,\modot$, $q=100$, observed for its final $10\,\hr$), we compute fitting factors between eccentric signals and circular templates, maximizing over the template's total mass and mass ratio with a differential-evolution search, for the B-DECIGO, LGWA-Si, and IndIGO-D noise curves and a flat PSD. The mismatch grows with initial eccentricity $e_0$ and crosses the standard $3\%$ threshold at $e_0\simeq3\times10^{-2}$, well within the range allowed by the waveform model and expected from dynamical formation. The best-fitting circular templates also bias the total mass and mass ratio by several percent at $e_0=0.1$. Combining the mismatch with the signal-to-noise-dependent distinguishability criterion, we find that for a source at $1\,\mathrm{Gpc}$, eccentricities as small as $e_0\simeq5\times10^{-4}$ (B-DECIGO and IndIGO-D) and $5\times10^{-3}$ (LGWA-Si) are resolvable, one to two orders of magnitude below where detection efficiency degrades. The loss of match arises from the excitation of radial Teukolsky harmonics, which spread power into sidebands that circular templates cannot represent, and from the slower orbital decay of eccentric binaries at fixed initial semi-latus rectum. Robust detection and parameter estimation of IMRIs with DECIGO, LGWA, and IndIGO-D will require eccentric waveform models and template banks.

cross.title: Why Cassini's Oval Could Not Replace Kepler's Ellipse?
cross.summary: In the later seventeenth century, Kepler's ellipse was not yet accepted. Ward claimed that Boulliau's conic hypothesis amounted to a Ptolemaic equant at the ellipse's empty focus, and built his own model on it. Around 1675--1680, Giovanni Domenico Cassini proposed another curve, the ``oval'', a genus-1 quartic with no closed-form Kepler equation; yet its eccentric anomaly shares exactly the leading coefficient of Kepler's, and its empty focus is, for the Sun, 38 times closer to a true equant than the ellipse's. Dynamically, Binet's formula shows that the force producing the oval under the area law departs from the inverse square by an index $\mathcal{D}(e)\sim3/(4e^2)$, depending on the oval's parameter $e$: no single exponent serves the whole family. This absence of universality, not of an area law, distinguishes it from the ellipse, and arguably explains why Cassini, the Académie and Leibniz kept the question open after the \emph{Principia} (1687).

cross.title: Non-Canonical Q-balls in Polyattractor Inflation Models
cross.summary: We show that Q-balls can exist in supergravity-based polyattractor inflation models that interpolate between $\alpha$-attractor T-models and polynomial attractor models. We consider both the original polyattractor potential and a natural generalisation. We find that Q-balls solutions exist when the model deviates significantly from the T-model $\alpha$-attractor, whereas in the T-model limit no Q-balls exist. These are non-canonical Q-balls due to the non-canonical kinetic term of the complex inflaton field. Such Q-balls could have significant cosmological consequences if they are produced at the end of inflation. In particular, if the global $\mathrm{U}(1)$ symmetry of the supergravity-based polyattractor model is unbroken, the Q-balls can be absolutely stable and could account for dark matter.

cross.title: Scaling of impact ripples across planetary conditions
cross.summary: Ubiquitous wind-driven (aeolian) ripples have been thought to emerge solely from grain collisions with the bed during saltation. Recent findings, however, have shown that there are two scales of aeolian ripples, with the larger scale having a hydrodynamic origin, akin to water ripples, and the smaller scale ('impact ripples') being hypothesized to emerge from the grain-bed collision mechanism. Still, there are several instances where only one ripple scale is found and the formation mechanism is not clear. Here we compare numerical simulations of only impact ripples with observations, over a broad range of planetary conditions, to clarify their defining characteristics. We find two main regimes for the scaling of impact ripple wavelengths based on transport intensity: for low-intensity transport ('saltation' regime), impact ripple wavelengths scale with grain size regardless of the fluid density; whereas for high-intensity transport ('collisional' regime) wavelengths scale with the average hoplength and thus increase with the fluid velocity. In contrast, impact ripple migration speeds strongly depend on the grain-fluid density ratio, grain size and fluid velocity. Finally, we find that impact ripple speeds become zero or negative (denoting stationary ripples and antiripples, respectively) for grain-fluid density ratios below a threshold that depends on the grain size. In particular, for low density ratios, like those found on Venus, or millimeter-scale grains on Earth, we find only antiripples. Our results thus provide a general framework for interpreting ripple emergence across environments and for identifying impact ripples in ambiguous field or experimental data.

repl.title: An Empirical Calibration of the Tip of the Red Giant Branch Distance Method in the Near Infrared. II. JWST NIRCam Wide Filters
repl.summary: The tip of the red giant (TRGB) is a standardizable candle and is identifiable as the discontinuity at the bright extreme of the red giant branch (RGB) stars in color-magnitude diagram (CMD) space. The TRGB-based distance method has been calibrated and used to measured distances to galaxies out to $D\leq20$ Mpc with the $I$-band equivalent Hubble Space Telescope ($HST$) $F814W$ filter, and as an important rung in the distance ladder to measure the Hubble constant, $H_0$. In the infrared (IR), the TRGB apparent magnitude ranges from $1-2$ magnitudes brighter than in the optical, and now with the IR James Webb Space Telescope ($JWST$) observatory the feasible distance range of the TRGB method can be extended to $\sim50$ Mpc. However, in the IR the TRGB luminosity depends to varying degrees on stellar metallicity and age. In this study we standardize the TRGB luminosity using stellar colors as a proxy for metallicity/age to derive color-based corrections for the $JWST$ Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) short wavelength (SW) filters $F090W$, $F115W$, $F150W$ and the long wavelength (LW) filters $F277W$, $F356W,$ and $F444W$. We provide recommended filter combinations for distance measurements depending on the requisite precision. For science requiring high precision ($\leq1\%$ in distance) and robustness we recommend measuring the TRGB in $F090W$ vs $F090W-F150W$ or $F115W$ vs. $F115W-F277W$ with the caveat that even with $JWST$ long integration times will be necessary at further distances. If lower precision ($>1.5\%$ in distance) can be tolerated, or if shorter integration times are desirable, we recommend measuring the TRGB in either $F115W$ or $F150W$ paired with $F356W$. We do not recommend $F444W$ for precision TRGB measurements due to its lower angular resolution.

repl.title: The Palomar 5 Stellar Stream in DESI Legacy Surveys DR10: Wide-field Morphology and Constraints on the Inner Halo Potential Shape
repl.summary: The Palomar 5 stellar stream probes the gravitational potential of the inner Milky Way, where the disk, dark halo, and time-dependent perturbations all contribute substantially to the force field. Using the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys Data Release 10 (DR10), we map the wide-field morphology of the stream over $-25^\circ<\phione<20^\circ$ and $-5^\circ<\phitwo<10^\circ$. Our analysis combines a cluster-calibrated PARSEC color--magnitude diagram filter, a continuous main-sequence turnoff plus RR Lyrae distance relation, and a field star response tied to local imaging depth. After applying the response correction, we recover the stream clearly over $-15.5^\circ\le\phione\le7.0^\circ$ and reveal no coherent low-surface-brightness extension beyond this range within our DR10 search footprint. Mock stream fits to the measured centroid and width yield an NFW potential flattening parameter $\qphiz=0.82^{+0.13}_{-0.11}$, assuming a static Hernquist bulge, a Miyamoto--Nagai disk, and a potential-flattened NFW halo with fixed $r_s=20\,{\rm kpc}$ and fixed $V_c(R_0)=232\,\kms$ at the Solar radius. The posterior favors an oblate effective inner halo potential, with a minor dependence on the assumed progenitor mass. The DR10 stream morphology therefore provides a homogeneous observational reference well suited for future joint analyses that incorporate density information, proper motions, line-of-sight velocities, and time-dependent perturbations.

repl.title: Baryonification II: Constraining feedback with X-ray and kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich observations
repl.summary: Baryonic feedback alters the matter distribution on small and intermediate scales, posing a challenge for precision cosmology. The new, component-wise baryonification (BFC) approach provides a self-consistent framework to model feedback effects for different observables. In this paper we use this framework to fit kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) observations from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) alongside halo X-ray gas fractions from eROSITA, investigating baryonic feedback in a cosmological context. We first show that the kSZ data from ACT is consistent with the gas fractions from eROSITA, both suggesting a feedback model that is stronger than what is assumed in most hydrodynamical simulations. This finding is in contrast to older, pre-eROSITA gas fraction measurements that point towards weaker feedback in tension with the kSZ results. We suspect these discrepancies to be due to selection bias in the pre-eROSITA sample, or differences in halo mass estimation between the two data sets. In a further step, we use the BFC model to predict the baryonic suppression of the matter power spectrum. Based on our combined fit to data from ACT and eROSITA, we find a power spectrum suppression that exceeds the percent-level at modes above $k=0.3-0.6 \,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, growing to 2-8 percent at $k=1\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, and to 20-25 percent at $k=5\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, consistent with strong-feedback hydrodynamical simulations. Finally, we compare our best-fitting model to the observed gas density and pressure profiles of massive galaxy clusters from the X-COP sample, finding excellent agreement. These results show that BFC provides a self-consistent picture of feedback across mass- and length scales as well as different cosmological observables, thus making it promising for applications to multiwavelength studies to jointly constrain cosmology and baryonic effects.

repl.title: Modeling stellar convective transport with plumes : II. Transport Properties of Locally and Non-locally driven Convection
repl.summary: We perform three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations of two idealized convection setups: a cooling-driven model (Model C) and an entropy-gradient-driven model (Model S). The two setups exhibit clear differences: while Model S develops large, relatively stationary eddies excited at depth, Model C is dominated near the surface by intermittent plume-like downflows that produce broad non-Gaussian velocity distributions and a turbulent energy flux that exceeds that in Model S by nearly an order of magnitude in the upper convection zone. Conventional gradient-diffusion (GD) closures reproduce the transport in Model S but significantly underestimate it in Model C, demonstrating that the plume-dominated transport realized in our cooling-driven setup cannot be reproduced by a local, gradient-based model. To address this, we introduce a Time-Space Double Averaging (TSDA) method that extracts coherent fluctuations, yielding a diagnostic variable $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}$ that peaks where the flux is largest. Building on this insight, we propose a modified GD closure in which the turbulent diffusivity is corrected by a plume-mediated term, achieving quantitative agreement with simulation results. Although the closure requires a calibrated model parameter and a careful choice of the averaging window, it provides a physically transparent framework that links coherent plume dynamics to mean-field transport and offers a pathway toward improved subgrid models for non-equilibrium stellar convection zones.

repl.title: When the Shadow Meets Its Measure: Assessing the Feasibility of Submillimeter Black Hole Shadow Imaging in Megamaser-disk Active Galactic Nuclei
repl.summary: Well-modeled water megamaser disks offer a path to black hole shadow (BHS) tests of strong-field gravity beyond Sgr A* and M87*: their very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) angular dynamics precisely constrains $M_\bullet/D$, the maser-disk orientation, and the dynamical center within the maser reference frame, thereby predicting the fiducial Schwarzschild BHS angular size without an externally adopted distance. We assess 21 megamaser galaxies as BHS targets using published maser measurements to calculate BHS angular sizes and baseline requirements. We combine new Submillimeter Array (SMA) continuum observations with archival Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and Very Large Array (VLA) measurements to estimate arcsecond-scale 230 GHz flux densities and identify the strongest nuclear-region sources for higher-resolution follow-up. We also estimate the maximum dust and extended-jet contributions, examine limited variability measurements, and, for the leading candidate NGC 4258, evaluate the astrometry required to detect a spin-dependent offset between the BHS center and the maser dynamical center. Only NGC 4258 has an adopted BHS angular size resolvable with an Earth--L2 baseline; the other adopted sizes require longer baselines, while an Earth--L4/L5 separation would be sufficient for all. Five sources reach $S_{230}\gtrsim10$ mJy. However, whether the observed 230 GHz emission arises on BHS scales and is sufficiently optically thin to reveal a BHS remains unknown throughout the sample. NGC 4258's submillimeter excess is consistent with a thin disk transitioning to an advection-dominated flow; its spin-offset test remains infeasible with present maser astrometry.

repl.title: Pulsar timing arrays: the emerging gravitational-wave landscape
repl.summary: Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments have found evidence for a nanoHertz gravitational wave (GW) background (GWB). The challenge is now to turn evidence for a GWB into an understanding of the sources and physics that produce it. This review connects the physics of the Hellings--Downs correlation to the interpretation of the GWB spectrum and anisotropy, asking whether supermassive black hole binary populations consistent with electromagnetic observations can explain the signal. Searches for individual binaries take these questions further: multi-messenger observations and pulsar terms can reveal the evolution of these binary systems. Realizing this potential requires reliable noise models and candidate validation. We explain how pulsar noise, unresolved sources, and incomplete sky coverage limit these inferences. The same PTA observations also probe cosmic strings and ultralight dark matter, while fitted timing parameters extend GW searches to picohertz frequencies and enable measurements of Galactic acceleration. Rapid data combination and the larger, more precisely timed arrays expected from the Square Kilometre Array Observatory and Deep Synoptic Array will increase the sensitivity of these searches and measurements, sharpening our view of the emerging GW landscape.

repl.title: Constraints on the Physical Association between ICECAT1 Neutrinos and Fast Radio Bursts Using the Second CHIME/FRB Catalogue
repl.summary: We present a search for neutrino counterparts to fast radio bursts (FRBs) using temporal and spatial cross-matching between the 1423 non-repeating FRBs of the Second CHIME/FRB catalogue and the 73 alerts of the IceCube high-energy alert-track catalogue ICECAT1 from 2018 July 25 to 2020 December 31. Because current FRB-neutrino models do not agree on the emission order, we adopt a two-sided temporal hypothesis and define the significance criterion from the expected number of chance coincidences before the search. We find no statistically significant association: no pair lies within the $3\sigma$ and $5\sigma$ coincidence windows of $3.50 \times 10^2$ s and $7.43 \times 10^{-2}$ s, and the pair closest in time, FRB20190630C-IC190629A, is consistent with a chance coincidence ($p = 0.254$, $0.66\sigma$). Using a population-level stacking analysis, we derive 90% upper limits on the neutrino-to-radio luminosity ratio of FRBs, $\xi \lesssim 1.4 \times 10^{11}$ for a neutrino spectral index $\gamma=1.0$ to $6.8 \times 10^{12}$ for $\gamma=3.0$, assuming neutrino emission within the burst duration. For a neutrino number spectrum $dN/d\epsilon \propto \epsilon^{-2}$, the corresponding limit on the neutrino fluence per burst is about a factor of 4 below those of previous stacking searches. For $\gamma=2$, the limits on the isotropic neutrino energy, $10^{49}$-$10^{52}$ erg, lie more than five orders of magnitude above the predictions of magnetar-driven shock models, so the present data do not constrain these models. Nevertheless, our blind significance criterion and population-stacking limits provide a baseline for future multi-messenger searches.

repl.title: OJALÁ: Optimizing J-PAS Astronomy for Large-scale Analysis. A transformer-based model for source classification and physical-parameter inference
repl.summary: The advent of large-scale surveys requires efficient machine learning techniques to exploit massive datasets. We present OJALA, a transformer-based autoregressive model that classifies astronomical objects and infers their physical parameters from 54-band J-PAS photometry combined with broad-band data from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys and WISE. The model is trained on approximately 20 million synthetic SEDs generated from DESI DR1 spectra and validated using a cross-matched sample of approximately 121,000 J-PAS and DESI objects. OJALA classifies stars, galaxies, and QSOs and estimates photometric redshifts for galaxies and QSOs. It recovers galaxy stellar masses and star formation rates, predicts optical emission-line equivalent widths and extinction-corrected H$\alpha$ luminosities, and reproduces the BPT and WHAN diagnostic diagrams. It also estimates stellar atmospheric parameters, including effective temperature and metallicity. Comparisons with dedicated multilayer perceptrons show that a single OJALA model generally matches or outperforms specialized predictors and remains robust under incomplete photometric coverage. We release the code, model weights, and a Value Added Catalog for the J-PAS Early Data Release.
